newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Health is Yeltsin's main concern on 66th birthday.
newsitem.headline: Health is Yeltsin's main concern on 66th birthday.

text.p: When President Boris Yeltsin turns 66 on Saturday, the traditional Russian birthday toasts of good health may be more heartfelt than ever.
Yeltsin's physical and political condition is at best shaky, seven months into a four-year second term in which he has spent more time in hospital than at the Kremlin.

His opponents say Russia is running on auto-pilot and are trying to banish the president into retirement. Even one of Yeltsin's loyal ministers has declared the past year a failure for economic reforms.
An opposition newspaper summed up its views this week by publishing a cartoon portraying a determined Yeltsin grappling with the wheel of the ship of state in his hospital bed.
Some critics say the whole political system is sick and the constitution should be amended to limit the president's powers.

"We have built an authoritarian power pyramid. As long as the president is at the top, the entire pyramid is moving and doing something," ousted security adviser Alexaander Lebed said in a newspaper interview this week.
"Now he has been still for half a year and everything has started crumbling. That is abnormal."
Little wonder that Yeltsin is planning only a quiet celebration with his family at the residence outside Moscow where he is recovering from pneumonia.

Yeltsin is several years past the average life expectation for Russian men, and a shadow of the instinctive and energetic leader who climbed onto a tank in August 1991 to help put down a hardline coup against then Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev.

The decline is obvious even since his 65th birthday. After a dramatic surge of energy during last year's election campaign, Yeltsin collapsed on the eve of his victory over communist Gennady Zyuganov in a runoff vote on July 3.
He disappeared from view, underwent heart surgery on November 5 and then went down with pneumonia this month. Television pictures of him this week showed him alert but slimmed-down and visibly aged.

Even so, Yeltsin's thoughts are on anything but retirement to the vegetable patch at his "dacha" in the country. His aides have tried to put down endless speculation over his health by saying he is raring to get back to full-time work.
Yeltsin and his Kremlin team look determined at all costs to prevent an early election which would provide an chance for Zyuganov or, more likely, Lebed to come to power.

His aides appear to believe that even if Yeltsin proved unable to run everyday affairs of state again, he would have an important role to play simply in occupying the seat which Lebed or Zyuganov want to grab from under him.
"It is clear that Yeltsin is very ill and can do only a few hours of work at a time, but that is probably enough," political analyst Sergei Markov said.
"He does not have to be running around the country any more. It is enough for him just to be there to keep out the others."

Under this scenario, Yeltsin is on hand to preside over the most important national decisions and his aides, led by Kremlin chief of staff Anatoly Chubais and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, are responsible for everyday affairs.
"In reality, Yeltsin's administration and government gets by quite well without him," said Viktor Kremenyuk, deputy head of the USA and Canada Institute thinktank.
Yeltsin's critics do not see it this way. They say political and economic reforms are on hold, as are foreign policy decisions, while the president is absent or ill.
Even Economy Minister Yevgeny Yasin, a Yeltsin ally, has criticised the lack of progress made in economic reforms in 1996, when attention was focused on the election.

"One has to say it (the economic reform programme) failed," Interfax news agency quoted Yasin as saying during a debate in parliament, adding that the only significant achievement last year had been to reduce inflation.

Despite the constant attacks on Yeltsin, he is under little immediate threat. Amending the constitution is a long and complicated procedure which most political experts say has at best an outside chance of success.
"It is easier to teach a crocodile to fly than to change this constitution," liberal politician Grigory Yavlinsky said.
For Yeltsin, the main threat in his 67th year looks set to remain his own health.
